h:
The King had grown impatient.

Each winter, frost crept across his orchards. The boughs hung bare. The ground hardened. Revenue stopped.

His ministers waited. His merchants waited. His sons waited.

The King did not wait.

He commissioned engineers. They built a glass dome, an arena of captured sky. It stretched across three hundred acres of orchard. Iron frames. Crystal panels. A cathedral to his will.

Beneath it, he lit fires. Not hearths, forges. Coal burned day and night. He hung ten thousand oil lamps from iron scaffolding, ablaze at all hours.

The trees blinked awake in the unnatural glow.

“Behold,” the King announced at midwinter harvest, “The Perpetual Summer. I have conquered the calendar itself.”

The first year, it seemed he had.

The trees, disoriented by constant warmth and light, bloomed in December. By February, branches bent under impossible fruit. Merchants arrived from distant kingdoms. Gold flooded the treasury.

His advisors composed ballads.

His priests called it providence.

His sons called him visionary.

The King walked his glowing orchard at midnight and smiled. He had done what no king before him dared: he had deleted winter.

The second year brought even greater yield.

The trees, confused but obedient, blossomed three times. Fruit hung beside flowers. Harvest became continuous. The King built warehouses. His wealth doubled.

But the trees were changing.

Bark grew thin. Pale. Almost translucent.

Branches thickened but felt hollow when struck.

Roots spread shallow, grasping at surface soil.

The foresters noticed but said nothing. Who questions a king in his triumph?

The third spring, though there was no spring, only endless summer, the trees refused to bloom.

Branches simply hung. Dormant. Defiant.

The King ordered more coal. Hotter fires. Brighter lamps.

By summer, leaves began to fall. Not autumn gold, gray. Brittle. Like burned paper.

Then came the sound.

A crack. Sharp as a whip.

Then another.

One of the great oaks, a tree that had stood for three generations, split down its center. The trunk twisted as it fell, spraying splinters across the glass dome. It struck the ground with a sound like thunder.

Within a week, twelve more fell.

Within a month, entire groves collapsed.

The King ran through the wreckage, his robes singed by the fires that still burned beneath the dome. He grabbed branches, shook trunks, screamed at the engineers.

“I gave you everything! Light! Heat! Constant growth! Why do you betray me?”

The trees said nothing.

The engineers examined the fallen timber. The wood was soft. Porous. It had grown quickly yes, but hollow. The grain was loose. The rings were faint, barely visible.

One old forester finally spoke:

“Majesty, the trees grew fat. But not strong. They never slept. They never hardened. Winter does not steal, it builds. The cold forces the sap inward. The darkness triggers dormancy. The freeze makes the wood dense, resilient, able to bear its own weight.”

He held up a piece of timber from the fallen oak.

“This wood has no strength. It never knew winter. It never learned to survive.”

The King stared at the rotted core.

“But I gave them more. More light. More warmth. More time to grow.”

“Yes, Majesty. And you gave them no time to become what they were meant to be.”

By the fourth year, the dome stood empty.

Every tree had collapsed or been cleared.

The fires were cold.

The lamps were dark.

The glass panels cracked from their own weight.

The King, older now and quieter, stood at the edge of the ruins.

Outside the dome, beyond the walls of his experiment, the wild orchards still stood. Gnarled. Weathered. Small.

But alive.

They had endured the winter he abolished. They had slept when he demanded wakefulness. They had grown slow when he commanded speed.

And they stood.

The King learned, too late, what the trees had always known:

You cannot cheat the rhythm.

You cannot delete the dark and keep the light.

You cannot extract endless growth without the season that builds strength.

The Perpetual Summer was not abundance.

It was hollow fruit on dying branches.

What nature demands, impatience cannot supply.

“To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted.” Ecclesiastes 3:1-2
